title: Views — Introduction
description: Learn what views are and why they are useful for simplifying queries and abstracting complexity.

data.text: A view is a named query stored in the database catalog that allows you to refer to it later. Think of a view as a saved SELECT statement that you can query like a table.

data.alt: SQL Server views diagram showing multiple tables feeding into a view

items: Security: Restrict users to access only a subset of data through a view.
Simplicity: Hide complex joins and conditions behind a simple view name.
Consistency: Encapsulate complex logic in one place so every query uses the same definition.

data.text: A view is defined with `CREATE VIEW` followed by a single `SELECT` statement. The query is stored in the catalog, not the rows it returns, so every time you query the view SQL Server re-runs the underlying `SELECT`.

data.title: Create and query a view
data.content: The view hides the join and the status filter behind a single name. `CREATE OR ALTER` lets you re-run the script safely.
data.code:
CREATE OR ALTER VIEW sales.vw_CompletedOrders
AS
SELECT
    c.CustomerID,
    c.CompanyName,
    o.SalesOrderID,
    o.OrderDate,
    o.TotalDue
FROM sales.Customer AS c
JOIN sales.SalesOrderHeader AS o
    ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
WHERE o.Status = 5;
GO

SELECT TOP (10) *
FROM sales.vw_CompletedOrders
ORDER BY OrderDate DESC;

data.title: Interview angle
data.text: A view is expanded into the calling query at compile time — it is not a cached result set. Chain too many views together and the optimizer has more work to do with less information. Keep views shallow, and index the base tables (or use an indexed view) when the query is hot.

data.title: Views Introduction Key Points
points: A view is a saved query stored in the database catalog.
Views do not store data (except indexed views).
Views provide security, simplicity, and consistency benefits.
You can query a view just like a table using SELECT.
